headline: Gold hits a record above 840 dollars
text: On 21 January the London gold fixing reached a record 843 dollars an ounce, three days after silver touched 49.45 dollars. Gold averaged 675 dollars in January, almost half as much again as in December. Buyers want metal instead of money after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, with American hostages still held in Tehran and consumer prices 13.3 percent higher in December than a year earlier.
imageCaption: A one-ounce Krugerrand, the South African gold coin popular with investors

headline: Boeing soars 29% as the Afghanistan invasion sends money into defence stocks
text: Boeing shares rose 29% in January, far ahead of a market up 6%. Soviet troops entered Afghanistan on 25 December, and with American diplomats still held hostage in Tehran, President Carter told Congress on 23 January that any attempt by an outside power to seize the Persian Gulf would be repelled by force, and asked for military spending to rise 5% a year above inflation for five years. Investors turned to the arms makers: Boeing builds the B-52 bombers and Minuteman missiles the Air Force relies on, and its air-launched cruise missile is in a fly-off against a rival design.

imageCaption: A Boeing E-3 Sentry airborne warning aircraft of the US Air Force
imageCredit: US Air Force, Tech. Sgt. John K. McDowell

headline: Sony takes its Walkman abroad
text: Sony began selling its Walkman outside Japan in February. The pocket cassette player cannot record: it only plays music, through light headphones, while you walk. In Japan, where it went on sale in July 1979 for about 33,000 yen, it sold more than 30,000 in its first two months, against the 5,000 a month Sony had planned. In some countries it is sold under other names, such as Stowaway in Britain and Soundabout in America.
imageCaption: The Sony Walkman TPS-L2, the original model, first sold in 1979

headline: Credit controls and the silver crash knock shares down 10 percent
text: On 14 March President Carter announced the first credit controls since the Second World War, with limits on lending, credit cards and instalment loans, as inflation and short-term interest rates both stood near 18 percent. On 27 March the silver market collapsed: silver fell to 10.80 dollars an ounce from over 50 in January after the Hunt brothers could no longer meet calls on their borrowed position, and trading in the shares of their broker Bache was suspended. The S&P 500 ended March at 102.09, down 10% in the month.

headline: Intel, the maker of the microprocessor, enters the game
text: Intel, a Californian company founded in 1968, built the first commercial microprocessor, a whole computer processor on one chip, in 1971, and its memory chips were the best-selling in the world in the early 1970s. In 1978 it brought out the 8086, a more powerful 16-bit processor. Memory chips are a tough, cyclical business with strong Japanese competition; processors are the newer bet.
imageCaption: Intel's Andy Grove, Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore with a chip layout, 1978

headline: Sandoz's cyclosporin used in a liver transplant
text: On 9 March Thomas Starzl in the United States used Sandoz's experimental drug cyclosporin in a liver transplant. Sandoz scientists discovered on 31 January 1972 that the substance, isolated from a soil fungus, damps the immune system, and doctors in Cambridge led by Roy Calne have shown promise in kidney transplants. It is still in trials.
imageCaption: Thomas Starzl, the Pittsburgh surgeon who pioneered liver transplants with cyclosporin

headline: Wal-Mart passes a billion dollars in yearly sales
text: Wal-Mart's sales for the business year that ended on 31 January reached about 1.25 billion dollars, against 44 million in 1970. No retailer has reached the billion-dollar mark so fast. In 1977 Forbes ranked it first among discount retailers for return on equity and for growth in sales and earnings.
imageCaption: Walton's Five and Dime, Bentonville, Arkansas, where Sam Walton began ;;

headline: America breaks with Iran, and a rescue mission dies in the desert
text: On 7 April the United States cut diplomatic relations with Iran and widened its sanctions. On 24 and 25 April a secret mission to free the hostages, Operation Eagle Claw, was called off in the Iranian desert; a helicopter then collided with a transport plane, killing eight American servicemen, and an Iranian civilian also died. Secretary of State Cyrus Vance resigned.
imageCaption: Wreckage at Desert One, the Iranian desert, after the failed hostage rescue attempt, April 1980

headline: Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett's holding company, enters the game
text: Berkshire Hathaway of Omaha began as a New England textile maker and now owns insurance companies, See's Candies, the Buffalo Evening News and 60% of Blue Chip Stamps, and invests its insurers' money in shares. In his annual letter of 3 March, chairman Warren Buffett reports book value of 335.85 dollars per share at the end of 1979, with shares held by the insurers counted at market value, up from 19.46 dollars when he took control in the mid-1960s. Berkshire pays no dividend and has never split its share, so one share costs a few hundred dollars.
imageCaption: Kiewit Plaza in Omaha, Nebraska, home of Berkshire Hathaway’s offices

headline: Riots at Zurich's opera house: 'Züri brännt'
text: On the night of 30 to 31 May several hundred young people clashed with police in front of the Zurich opera house, joined by a crowd coming from a Bob Marley concert. The city council had just approved 60 million francs to renovate the opera house while turning down the young people's demand for an autonomous youth centre. Students filmed the first night of rioting.
imageCaption: Bob Marley in concert at the Hallenstadion, Zurich, 30 May 1980, the evening of the opera house riots

headline: Rates tumble in the recession and gold bounces back
text: Interest rates are falling as fast as they rose. Banks cut the prime rate to 12 percent on 17 June, from 20 percent in early April, and the rate banks charge each other averaged under 9.5 percent in June against 17.6 percent in April. The Fed has cut its discount rate from 13 percent. Gold rebounded and averaged 601 dollars, 17 percent more than in May.
imageCaption: The Federal Reserve Board building, Washington

headline: The Walkman reaches America
text: Sony's pocket stereo cassette player, the TPS-L2, went on sale in the United States in June under the name Soundabout. Abroad it is also sold as the Stowaway in Britain and the Freestyle in Sweden and Australia.
imageCaption: The Sony Walkman TPS-L2, the first model, 1979

headline: Iraq invades Iran
text: On 22 September Iraqi aircraft struck ten Iranian airfields, and the next day Iraqi troops crossed the border along a front of more than 600 kilometres, aiming above all at the oil province of Khuzestan and the Shatt al-Arab waterway. Saddam Hussein had torn up the 1975 border agreement with Iran days before. Iran, its army purged after the revolution, is fighting back with regular troops, Revolutionary Guards and volunteers. Oil output from both countries is disrupted.
imageCaption: Smoke rises over Tehran's Mehrabad airport after Iraqi air strikes, 22 September 1980

headline: Reagan's victory sets off a rally; the Dow is back above 1,000
text: Shares jumped after Ronald Reagan won the presidential election on 4 November. About two weeks after the vote the Dow Jones average closed above 1,000 for the first time since the end of 1976, and on 20 November the S&P 500 closed at a record 140.40. The S&P 500 gained 10% in November, to 140.52.
imageCaption: Ronald Reagan greets supporters on a campaign stop in Indiana, 1980

headline: Reagan beats Carter in a landslide
text: Ronald Reagan won the US presidency on 4 November with 489 electoral votes to 49 and about 51 percent of the vote to Carter's 41, carrying 44 states. He promises tax cuts, less regulation and a harder line with Moscow. Shares jumped: the day after the vote the New York Stock Exchange traded a record 84 million shares, and the Dow climbed back above 1,000 for the first time since 1976.
imageCaption: President Carter welcomes President-elect Reagan and Nancy Reagan to the White House, 20 November 1980

headline: Schlumberger ranks among the world's most valuable companies
text: After Reagan's election, buying on Wall Street concentrated on oil and defence shares, and Schlumberger rose 20 percent in the month. With a market value of about 25 billion dollars, the oilfield-services company ranks fourth by market value behind AT&T, IBM and Exxon, valued at about 25 times its earnings and nearly eight times its book value.
imageCaption: The Schlumberger Well Surveying Corporation building, Houston

headline: Apple Computer, maker of the Apple II, goes public
text: Apple Computer went public on 12 December: 4.6 million shares at 22 dollars raised over 100 million dollars, the biggest offering since Ford in 1956, and by the close they traded at 29. It makes the Apple II, a small computer for homes, schools and offices; sales were 118 million dollars in its last financial year. The founders, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, and about 300 others became millionaires.
imageCaption: The Apple II personal computer, introduced 1977

headline: The prime rate hits a record 21.5 percent
text: Major banks raised the prime rate to a record 21 percent on 16 December and to 21.5 percent on the 19th; in July it was 11 percent. The rate banks charge each other averaged nearly 19 percent in December, and the Fed has raised its discount rate back to about 13 percent. Consumer prices in November were 12.6 percent higher than a year earlier. Gold averaged 538 dollars, 14 percent less than in November.
imageCaption: Paul Volcker, chairman of the Federal Reserve
